title: Kiss the joy
hookLine: Mary in the garden is told 'touch me not' and sent running; Blake: kiss the joy as it flies
tomorrow: an emperor's private notebook opens with thank-yous. to whom?

cards: The last night of a trip, someone always says: let's not go home. In John's Gospel, early on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene stands weeping outside an empty tomb.
A man asks why she's crying; she thinks he's the gardener. Then he says her name, Mary, and she knows him. She turns: Rabboni, teacher.
And the next words she hears, in the King James Version, are: "Touch me not; for I am not yet ascended to my Father."

teach.b: Christians read that line in different ways. In Latin it's noli me tangere, and one old reading is: don't cling to me. She can't keep him the old way.
Instead she's given a job: "go to my brethren." Her joy doesn't stay in her hands. It runs to the others.
Some Christian writers called her the apostle to the apostles, the one sent to tell the ones who'd be sent.

Centuries later, the poet William Blake wrote four lines in a notebook that sound like that garden: "He who binds to himself a joy / Does the winged life destroy; / But he who kisses the joy as it flies / Lives in eternity's sun rise."
That's Blake's teaching here: eternity isn't later. It's met inside the passing moment, as long as you don't strangle it.
Elsewhere he says it as holding "Eternity in an hour." Look at Blake's verb for the right way to hold a joy: kiss. Not catch, not keep.
A joy bound tight dies like a caught butterfly.
A joy kissed as it flies keeps living, and so does the one who let it go.

how: Christians read Jesus's 'touch me not' to Mary Magdalene (John 20:17) in several ways, often as 'do not cling'; she is sent to tell the disciples. Blake's 'Eternity' (He who binds to himself a joy) is a short notebook poem on letting joy go free.

o: grabbing a happy moment so it can't slip away
saying goodbye to joy so you won't miss it later
enjoying a good thing fully, then letting it go

games.q: the garden and the poem: tap the pairs.
p: kisses the joy as it flies

s: in John's Gospel, Mary first thinks Jesus is the gardener
she knows him only when he says her name.
Blake's poem says to catch a joy and keep it safe
binding a joy destroys the winged life; kiss it as it flies.
Christians all read "touch me not" the same way
it's read in different ways; one old reading is "don't cling to me".

games.q: your best friend got her dream job across the country and leaves next week. you're thrilled, and gutted. what would Blake's lines suggest?
o: love the last week fully, then let her go with your blessing.
talk her into staying, so the friendship can stay exactly as it is.
pull back now, so it hurts less when she finally leaves.
games.why: "he who kisses the joy as it flies / Lives in eternity's sun rise." binding it, or pulling away from it, both lose the joy.

practice: Hold something light in your open palm: a leaf, a feather, a scrap of paper. Feel how little it weighs, and don't close your fingers around it. As the sit ends, tip your hand and let it fall.

wordCard.voice: Kiss the joy: loving a good thing fully without clutching it, Blake's joy kissed as it flies.

orig.note: Latin: touch me not, or do not cling to me (John 20:17 in the Vulgate).

carryVoice: Something to keep: as it flies, a joy held in an open hand. Day seventeen forty-seven, done.
